p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text describes how Bellinghast’s group matches phages to infections, and then how far the results so far reach. C names both strands. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the right answer must cover all its main parts, not just one paragraph.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 tells of a match that failed: “Ninety plates came back cloudy.” Paragraph 2 describes the collection and how often it finds a match. Paragraph 3 gives a small series of patients and what it cannot prove. Paragraph 4 sets a hopeful idea about escape mutants against a count of them, and paragraph 5 names what has improved and the trial that “will decide whether the treatment becomes ordinary”.

steps.title: Name the two strands
steps.text: Two strands run through the paragraphs: how a phage is matched to one patient’s bacteria, and how far the evidence so far reaches. The right answer must name both.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C names both strands. A turns the opening case into the subject of the whole text, B turns the sources of one collection into a claim about medicine in general, and D brings in how fast resistant bacteria spread, which the text never discusses.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about matching phages to infections and how far the results reach. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The text opens with an infected knee replacement that ends with the knee coming out, so implants and surgery stay in the mind.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never explains why implants become infected. The removed knee, and the eleven patients who “had the implant taken out anyway”, are outcomes in the story of matching and testing phages, not its subject (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text names “sewage outfalls, hospital drains” among the places where the phages were gathered, and phages are used as a treatment.
distractors.why_wrong: Those places supplied this one collection. The text never says that they have become the leading source of new medicines; it names them only to say where the collection came from.

distractors.why_tempting: The patient in the opening case had been through “four antibiotics”, so resistance to drugs seems to be the background of the whole text.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never compares the spread of resistant bacteria with the arrival of new antibiotics. Its question is narrower: whether a matched phage helps, and how anyone could tell (step 3).

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions, map the text paragraph by paragraph and look for the option that covers every main part. Here each paragraph adds to one of two strands: how phages are matched, and what the results can show.
p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A vivid opening case is often not the main subject. The failed match for the knee leads into the text; it is one example of the matching that the rest of the text is about.

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The text says that over five years “the collection has produced a usable match for rather more than half of the isolates sent to it”. An isolate is a bacterial sample, so D says the same. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the collection, so the answer must be stated in the text. The collection is described in the second paragraph.

steps.title: Find the figures
steps.text: The paragraph gives several numbers: “1,140 phages gathered since 2016”, of which “some four hundred have been sequenced and described in full”, and a match rate: “rather more than half of the isolates sent to it”.

steps.title: Read the match rate
steps.text: The glossary explains that an isolate is “a bacterial sample grown from one patient and kept as a pure culture”. So rather more than half of the samples sent to the collection find a usable match, which is what D says.

steps.title: Read the spread
steps.text: The same sentence adds that the figure “hides a spread: close to three in four for Klebsiella, well under half for the staphylococci that dominate infected implants”. Klebsiella and staphylococci are two kinds of bacteria.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D restates the match rate. A swaps the two rates and adds a result for implants, B turns “rather more than half” into every strain, and C turns the four hundred sequenced phages into phages given to patients; the text never says how many have been given to patients.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The collection finds a usable match for rather more than half of the samples sent to it. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Both kinds of bacteria and both rates are in the text, in one sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: A swaps the rates. The text gives Klebsiella “close to three in four” and the staphylococci “well under half”. It also never says that implant infections respond well: the staphylococci, the harder group to match, are the ones that “dominate infected implants” (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: The collection is large and still growing, so it sounds as if it should cover every strain in the end.
distractors.why_wrong: The text gives a match rate of “rather more than half”, not all. And the strain from the opening paragraph still has no match: “Two hundred phages have joined the collection since; none of them clears it.”

distractors.why_tempting: The number four hundred really is in the paragraph about the collection.
distractors.why_wrong: The four hundred are the phages that “have been sequenced and described in full”: their genetic code has been read and they have been studied in detail. The text never says how many phages have been given to patients (step 2).

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: For “What are we told about …” questions, find the paragraph about the named thing and check what each number counts. The right option keeps both the number and what it refers to.
p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: A real number attached to the wrong thing is the trap here. The figure of some four hundred counts phages that were sequenced, not phages given to patients, and the higher match rate belongs to Klebsiella, not to the staphylococci.

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: Of the sixty-three patients, “in forty-one the infection was under control at six months”, which is about two thirds, and “Every patient in it was also on antibiotics”. A says both. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about the sixty-three patients in the published series, so the answer must be stated in the text. The series is described in the third paragraph.

steps.title: Find the results
steps.text: “A series published last year followed sixty-three patients treated at four hospitals between 2020 and 2024; in forty-one the infection was under control at six months, and eleven had the implant taken out anyway.”

steps.title: Find the conditions
steps.text: The next sentence adds: “Every patient in it was also on antibiotics, since withholding them would have been indefensible, and the hospitals had referred the cases they judged most likely to respond.”

steps.title: Do the arithmetic
steps.text: Two thirds of sixty-three is forty-two, so forty-one is about two thirds. “Alongside antibiotics” matches the fact that every patient was also on antibiotics.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches both facts. B ignores the eleven implants that were taken out, C turns round the kind of cases that were referred, and D adds a comparison that the series did not have.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: About two thirds of the patients had the infection under control at six months, and all were also on antibiotics. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Forty-one good results stand out, and a reader who stops there may think that the treatment worked for everyone.
distractors.why_wrong: The same sentence says that “eleven had the implant taken out anyway” (step 2), so not all of them kept the implant.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence about the referrals does talk about which cases were chosen, so C seems to come from it.
distractors.why_wrong: C has it the wrong way round. The hospitals “had referred the cases they judged most likely to respond”, not the most difficult ones, and the text never says which patients in the series did best (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: A published medical study is often expected to compare treated patients with others, and the text does mention a randomised trial.
distractors.why_wrong: The series had no such comparison: “without a comparison group, a recovery in a patient taking four drugs says little about the fifth”. The randomised trial is a different study, which is only now enrolling patients.

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: For detail questions with figures, find the sentence that gives them, do any arithmetic yourself, and check every part of the option against the text.
p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Watch out for an option that reverses a detail from the right sentence. The text does discuss which cases were referred, but C turns “most likely to respond” into the most difficult cases.

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The hopeful story says that an escape mutant “ought to” be weaker. Of thirty-four escape mutants, nine had paid that price and twenty-five had not. So the hope holds for a minority, not as a rule, which is C. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that the answer is not stated outright; here you must compare the hopeful story with the numbers that test it.

steps.title: Find the hope
steps.text: Paragraph 4 sets out the hope: “The molecule is often one the bacterium needs as well, so an escape mutant ought to hold less firmly to an implant, or to become vulnerable again to an antibiotic it had shrugged off.” An escape mutant is a bacterium that has changed so that the phage no longer works on it, usually by altering the molecule the phage grips.

steps.title: Find the test
steps.text: Then come the numbers: “Bellinghast’s group sequenced thirty-four escape mutants recovered from patients during treatment. Nine had paid a price of that kind. The other twenty-five clung to plastic and grew as strongly as the strains they came from.”

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: Nine of thirty-four is about one in four. The price is real in some escape mutants, so the hope is not empty; but most of the thirty-four did not pay it, so it cannot be relied on as a rule.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches the numbers. A makes the price universal with “always”, D denies it entirely although nine mutants paid it, and B hands the question to the trial, which will decide something else.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The weakening happens in a minority of escape mutants, not as a rule. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The text explains why escape could cost a bacterium something, so the hope can sound proven.
distractors.why_wrong: The mechanism is only a hope: the text says that an escape mutant “ought to” be weaker. When the group checked, only nine of thirty-four had paid such a price (step 3), so escape does not always cost the bacterium something.

distractors.why_tempting: The trial is the text’s named test for the future, and “probably” makes the option sound careful.
distractors.why_wrong: The trial will decide “whether the treatment becomes ordinary”. Nothing in the text links it to what escape costs a bacterium, so the text gives no reason to think that it will probably settle that question. The evidence on the hope comes from the thirty-four escape mutants that Bellinghast’s group has already sequenced (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Twenty-five of the thirty-four mutants grew as strongly as before, so the hope can seem to have failed completely.
distractors.why_wrong: D says that none of the mutants was weakened, but “Nine had paid a price of that kind” (step 3). The hope holds for some of them, just not for most.

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a text sets out a hope or a theory and then reports a count, compare the part with the whole. A result like nine out of thirty-four supports a claim about some cases, not about all of them or none of them.
p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: A and D each read only one part of the result. A keeps the nine and forgets the twenty-five; D keeps the twenty-five and forgets the nine.

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer takes the work seriously but will not let the results so far decide the matter: Bellinghast’s caution is “warranted”, and “that trial, not any series, will decide whether the treatment becomes ordinary”. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s own attitude, not Bellinghast’s or Quilvey’s. Look for sentences in which the writer judges in the writer’s own voice.

steps.title: Find the writer’s judgements
steps.text: There are few, and they point the same way. At the end of the first paragraph, the writer warns that failed cases “rarely reach print, which is worth saying before any of the numbers that follow”. On Bellinghast’s caution: “the care is warranted: without a comparison group, a recovery in a patient taking four drugs says little about the fifth.”

steps.title: Find the verdict on routine use
steps.text: In the last paragraph the writer says what will settle the question: “that trial, not any series, will decide whether the treatment becomes ordinary”. The writer also credits a real gain, the faster delivery of preparations, as “The part of all this that has genuinely improved”.

steps.title: Read the attitude
steps.text: The writer reports the work in detail and credits real progress, so “Interested” fits. The writer waits for the trial, so the results so far do not settle the question. That is B, in both halves.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B fits both halves. A calls the approach a distraction, which the writer never does; C gives the writer Quilvey’s view; D ignores the writer’s own judgements.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer is interested but waits for the trial. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer opens on a failure and stresses how thin the record is, which can sound dismissive.
distractors.why_wrong: Doubt about the evidence is not dismissal. The writer never calls the approach a distraction, and credits a real improvement in the last paragraph: the median time to a preparation fell from nineteen days to six (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Quilvey’s view is given at length and without criticism, close to the writer’s own sentences.
distractors.why_wrong: That view is Quilvey’s own: Quilvey “is readier than that” and “would offer a matched phage as a standard option in infected joint replacements”. The writer does not join it, and puts the decision in the trial instead (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer reports both caution and readiness, so the text can read like a neutral report.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer does judge: Bellinghast’s care “is warranted”, and the trial, “not any series”, will decide (steps 2 and 3). A detached reporter with no view would not write those sentences.

p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, collect the writer’s own judging words, such as “worth saying” and “warranted”, and keep them apart from what named people think. Then check both halves of a two-part option.
p5-elf-b15-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: The strongest opinion in a text may belong to a person the writer reports on. Quilvey would offer a matched phage as a standard option in infected joint replacements; the writer waits for the trial.

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: To spare someone’s feelings is to take care not to hurt them. Under the rule, “every card without a date on it comes down” on the first Monday of the month, and the next sentence describes trade cards coming down even sooner, so a rule that spares nobody’s feelings fits. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “The rule ___ nobody’s feelings.” Just before it, the rule is set out: “on the first Monday of the month, every card without a date on it comes down.”

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: English speaks of sparing someone’s feelings: taking care not to hurt or embarrass them. A rule that spares nobody’s feelings is applied without that care. The next sentence fits this strict picture: a card advertising guttering repairs “is lucky to see a fortnight”.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To serve is usually to work for someone or to meet a need, as a rule might serve a purpose. To save is usually to rescue something or keep it from loss; to save someone something is to keep them from it, as in saving someone a journey. To spoil is usually to ruin something, as when news spoils a surprise. Save comes closest in meaning, but the common way to say that people are kept from being hurt is to spare their feelings, so “spares” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The rule spares nobody’s feelings”: it does not hold back for anyone. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A rule can serve a purpose, so “serves” sounds natural after “The rule”.
distractors.why_wrong: To serve is usually to work for someone or to meet a need. The sentence is about whether the rule holds back from hurting people, and the common expression for that is to spare someone’s feelings (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Saves” is close in meaning: to save someone something is to keep them from it.
distractors.why_wrong: Save is near in meaning, but the common expression for keeping people from being hurt is to spare their feelings, so “spares” fits better (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: “Spoils” is a negative word, so it seems to suit a strict rule.
distractors.why_wrong: To spoil something is usually to ruin it, as when news spoils a surprise. Read that way, the sentence would say that the rule hurts nobody, which does not fit the strict rule that the sentences around the gap describe (step 2).

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap is followed by an object such as “nobody’s feelings”, look for the verb that forms a common expression with it – here, to spare someone’s feelings.
p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: “Saves” and “spares” are close in meaning, so the choice rests on the expression, not on the general idea. Test each verb with the whole object: “___ nobody’s feelings”.

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: To get short shrift is to be dealt with quickly and with little patience. The rest of the sentence shows this: a trade card “is lucky to see a fortnight”, while a churchyard card “may stay up all summer”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Anything with a price on it gets short ___, so a card advertising guttering repairs is lucky to see a fortnight, while a card asking for help with the churchyard may stay up all summer.” Guttering is the channels that carry rainwater off a roof, and a fortnight is two weeks.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The words “so a card … is lucky to see a fortnight” show what the gap means: trade cards come down fast. English has an expression for being dealt with quickly and without much patience: to get short shrift. The noun shrift is old, and today it is met mostly in this expression.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: Thrift is usually careful use of money. Drift is usually slow movement, or the general meaning of what someone says. A shift is usually a period of work, or a change. Thrift may seem to fit because the cards have a price on them, and shift looks and sounds very like shrift. But the sentence is about how quickly trade cards are taken down, and short shrift is the expression for that, so “shrift” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Anything with a price on it gets short shrift.” The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Thrift is about money, and the sentence is about cards with “a price on it”.
distractors.why_wrong: Thrift is usually careful use of money. The sentence is about how long trade cards stay up, not about saving money, and the expression for quick, impatient treatment is short shrift (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Drift” rhymes with the key and is a common word.
distractors.why_wrong: Drift is usually slow movement, or the general meaning of what someone says. Neither of these says that trade cards come down quickly, which is what the rest of the sentence describes (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Shift” looks and sounds almost the same as the key, and it is a much more common word.
distractors.why_wrong: A shift is usually a period of work, or a change. The sentence needs the expression for being dealt with quickly and impatiently, and that expression is short shrift (step 2).

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: Use the clause after the gap. Here “so” introduces the result – a trade card is lucky to see a fortnight – and that result tells you what “gets short ___” must mean.
p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Look-alike words are the trap: “shift” and “thrift” differ from the key by a letter or two. Check that the whole expression makes sense, not just its sound.

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: “Not neighbourliness but ___” needs something set against neighbourliness. The next sentences say that a card with no reply “has only gone unread”, which a person can live with. Taking no interest, not caring, is indifference. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “These are errands too small to be worth arranging any other way, and what makes them possible is not neighbourliness but ___.” Neighbourliness is friendly help between neighbours.

steps.title: Follow the contrast
steps.text: “Not … but” sets the gap against neighbourliness, and the next two sentences say what it is: “A card that draws no reply has not been refused. It has only gone unread, and being unread is something a person can live next door to.” Nobody has to say no: a card can simply go unread, and a person can live with that. What makes the small requests possible is that people are free to take no notice of them, and taking no interest is indifference.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: Interference is usually getting involved where you are not wanted. Deference is polite respect, often shown by giving way to someone. An inference is a conclusion that you reach by reasoning. The sentences after the gap describe a card that simply goes unread, which is neither getting involved, nor showing respect, nor reasoning. So “indifference” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: What makes the errands possible “is not neighbourliness but indifference”. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Interference” ends in -ference like the key, and a noticeboard deals with other people’s business.
distractors.why_wrong: Interference is usually getting involved where you are not wanted. The text describes the opposite: a card that draws no reply “has only gone unread” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: After “neighbourliness”, a second polite word such as “deference” seems to belong.
distractors.why_wrong: Deference would put another kind of politeness in place of neighbourliness, but nothing after the gap is about respect. The next sentences describe cards that simply go unread (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Inference” looks very like the key: both start with in- and end in -ference.
distractors.why_wrong: An inference is a conclusion reached by reasoning. Nothing in the paragraph is about reasoning; it is about cards that can be left unread without anyone being refused (step 2).

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a gap follows “not … but”, the gap names something different from the first idea. Read on: the next sentences often say what it is.
p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: All four options end in -ference, so their shape gives nothing away. “Deference” is a trap because it sounds as kind as neighbourliness, but the sentences after the gap are about cards going unread, not about respect.

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: To come to nothing is to fail, to have no result. The sentence before says that nobody writes down “what came of it”, and the gapped sentence says that most cards end with no result. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Most of what goes up ___ to nothing.” What goes up are the cards pinned on the board.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: Just before, the writer says: “Nobody writes down what was asked for, and nobody writes down what came of it, so there is no telling whether the ladder was ever lent.” The gapped sentence is about results too. English says that a plan or an effort comes to nothing when it fails and has no result.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To carry is usually to hold something and take it somewhere. To cut is usually to divide something or make it smaller. To count is to add up, or to matter; something that counts for nothing has no importance. That last expression is close, but it is about importance and is followed by “for”, while this frame is about results and is followed by “to”. So “comes” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Most of what goes up comes to nothing.” The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Carries” appears in expressions such as carry weight, which are about whether something counts.
distractors.why_wrong: To carry is usually to hold something and take it somewhere. The sentence needs a verb for what the cards end in, and to come to nothing is to end with no result (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Something can be cut down to almost nothing, so “cuts” seems to go with “to nothing”.
distractors.why_wrong: To cut is usually to divide something or make it smaller, and nobody is making the cards smaller. The sentence before is about results – “what came of it” – and to come to nothing is to have no result (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Counting for nothing, having no importance, is a real expression, so “counts” sounds familiar here.
distractors.why_wrong: To count for nothing is to have no importance, and that expression is followed by “for”. This frame is about results, as “what came of it” shows, and its word is “to”: most of the cards come to nothing (step 2).

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: Check the small word after the gap. Here “to nothing” and the earlier “what came of it” both point to one expression: come to nothing.
p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: “Counts” is the closest trap, because count for nothing is a real expression. Check both the meaning and the preposition in the frame.

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The sentence before calls the board “indefensible on ordinary grounds”, yet nobody has proposed replacing it. The second fact goes against what the first would lead you to expect, so the gap needs “Nonetheless”, meaning in spite of that. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, no one in Denhollow has proposed replacing it, and the cards still go up as they always have.”

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The sentence before lists the board’s faults: it is “unaccountable, unmeasured, and administered by one man with a jam jar”. Unaccountable means that nobody has to answer for it, and administered means run. Faults like these would lead you to expect a proposal to replace the board, yet none has come. A sentence that goes against what came before needs a contrast word: “Nonetheless”, meaning in spite of that.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: As a link between sentences, “Accordingly” means for that reason. “Furthermore” adds another point in the same direction. “Correspondingly” means in a matching way. The faults do not explain why the board stays, the gapped sentence is not one more fault, and nothing in it matches the faults. So “Nonetheless” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Nonetheless, no one in Denhollow has proposed replacing it.” The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Accordingly” sounds formal and links the long list of faults to what follows.
distractors.why_wrong: As a link between sentences, “Accordingly” means for that reason. It would make the faults the reason why nobody replaces the board, but faults like these would be a reason to replace it (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph has been piling up points against the board, so another adding word seems natural.
distractors.why_wrong: “Furthermore” adds a point in the same direction. The gapped sentence is not another fault: it says that the board carries on and that nobody has proposed replacing it (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Correspondingly” is as formal as the key and sounds like a careful link.
distractors.why_wrong: “Correspondingly” means in a matching way. That nobody has proposed a replacement does not match the faults; it goes against them (step 2).

p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: For a connective gap, decide whether the gapped sentence follows from the one before, adds to it, or goes against it. When something “indefensible” carries on anyway, the link is a contrast.
p5-elf-b15-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: A long list before the gap can make an adding word or a result word feel natural. Read what the gapped sentence actually says before you choose.

p5-elf-b15-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Vessholm’s log counts 39 buckles, and “two in three came in the eight weeks after ballast work”. The ballast work is the tamping machine’s, so B says the same in other words. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the buckles in Vessholm’s log, so the answer must be stated in the text. The log is described near the end of the passage.

steps.title: Find the log
steps.text: “His log runs to 39 buckles – track shoved sideways out of line – across 19 summers, and two in three came in the eight weeks after ballast work.” A buckle, as the words between the dashes explain, is track pushed sideways out of line.

steps.title: Link the work to the machine
steps.text: The ballast work is described earlier: “A tamping machine lifts the track and packs new stone underneath, and for eight weeks afterwards that stone is loose.” So the eight weeks after ballast work are the weeks after a tamping machine has been through, and two in three is two thirds.

steps.title: Understand the words
steps.text: Ballast is the stone packed around the sleepers, the beams that the rails rest on. Welded rail cannot expand into gaps, so whether its force “goes anywhere is settled by stone”. That is why the weeks after new stone is packed matter.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B restates the tally. A adds gangs that usually came to work the ballast after a buckle, which the text never says; C turns “two in three” into all of them; and D ties most of the buckles to the hottest weeks, which the text never says.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Two thirds of the buckles came in the eight weeks after a tamping machine had been through. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence says that gangs are sent wherever somebody has reported something, so ballast work after a buckle sounds likely.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that ballast work followed a buckle. The sentence about gangs explains why “the quieter miles go uncounted”; it never says that a buckle brought a gang to work the ballast, usually or at all.

distractors.why_tempting: C keeps the eight weeks and the tamping machine, so it reads like a faithful summary.
distractors.why_wrong: The log says “two in three”, not all. About a third of the 39 buckles came at other times (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Heat makes rails push harder, so it seems natural that most buckles fell in the hottest weeks.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says this. It ties two in three of the buckles to the eight weeks after ballast work (step 2), and it adds: “The hottest week on record produced none.”

p5-elf-b15-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “What are we told about …” questions, find the sentence about the named thing and match each part of the option: the number, what it counts and when it happened. Reject any part that the text never states, however likely it sounds.
p5-elf-b15-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Common sense says that heat alone causes buckles, but the text says that whether the force goes anywhere “is settled by stone”. Answer from the log, not from what seems likely.

p5-elf-b15-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: In its best year the bar took less than a tollman’s yearly wage. But in the summer when it stood empty, takings at the main gate fell “by several times that wage”. So leaving it unmanned cost more than the bar took in any year. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the answer is not stated outright; here you must put the text’s figures side by side.

steps.title: Find the bar’s takings
steps.text: “It never paid for itself. In its best year it took less than the yearly wage of the tollman who sat there”. Takings are the money collected, and a tollman is the person who collected the tolls.

steps.title: Find the summer without a tollman
steps.text: In 1831 the bar was left unmanned for the summer, and “Takings at the main gate fell that season by several times that wage, while the trust's other two gates took what they usually took.” Even its best year brought the bar less than one wage, so a loss of several wages in one summer is more than the bar took in any year.

steps.title: See a likely reason
steps.text: The text does not say why the main gate lost money, but the lane suggests a reason: it “rejoined the turnpike well beyond the main gate”. With nobody at the bar, traffic could perhaps take the lane, pay nothing at the empty bar and miss the main gate. A turnpike is a toll road, and the trust was the body that ran it.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C puts the two figures together. A picks traffic that went through free, B judges the bar only by its own takings, and D blames the season, although the other two gates took their usual amounts.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Leaving the bar unmanned cost the main gate more than the bar took in any year. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The bar stood on the farm lane, and the two farms’ carts are the lane’s most obvious traffic.
distractors.why_wrong: Those carts paid nothing: “carts going about the two farms' business went through free, as the Act required”. So the farms’ carting was not traffic that the bar could charge.

distractors.why_tempting: Its first half sounds right: in its best year the bar took less than a tollman’s wage. And the board did agree to leave it empty.
distractors.why_wrong: Neither half holds once the main gate is counted. The bar’s own takings never covered the wage, but without a tollman the main gate lost “several times that wage” (step 3), so a tollman was worth paying. And “By September a man was back at Quarnley”.

distractors.why_tempting: A bad season can lower takings at any gate, so the season sounds like a sensible explanation.
distractors.why_wrong: The season cannot explain it: in the same summer “the trust's other two gates took what they usually took” (step 3). Besides the empty bar itself, only the main gate’s takings fell.

p5-elf-b15-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “suggest” questions with figures, put the numbers side by side and look for a comparison that the text never makes itself. A control – here the other two gates – tells you what the cause was not.
p5-elf-b15-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Judging something only by its own takings can mislead. The bar never paid for itself, yet leaving it empty cost the main gate several times a tollman’s yearly wage in a single summer.

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Of the hosing trial the text says: “It made no difference. One washed lot even read a little higher than the block beside it”. B says both things. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the blocks that were hosed down, so the answer must be stated in the text. The trial is described in the first paragraph.

steps.title: Find the trial
steps.text: Pemberdine “made a trial of it: two blocks washed down, two left alone, all four picked and fermented in the same shed that afternoon.” A block is an area of vines, and to ferment the grapes is to turn their juice into wine.

steps.title: Find the result
steps.text: “It made no difference. One washed lot even read a little higher than the block beside it, though Pemberdine will not build on a single pair.” To read higher is to give a higher measurement in the laboratory.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B gives both facts. A turns a time from the next paragraph into a rule about washing, C says that the washed fruit held less, and D gives Pemberdine a cause that the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Washing made no difference, and one washed lot even read a little higher. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does mention “a day or two”, and “some” makes A sound careful.
distractors.why_wrong: “A day or two” is the time Pemberdine gives before the smoke is held in a locked form, not a time for washing. The smoke compounds “cross the waxy skin of a grape within hours”, and the text never says that hosing removed any smoke.

distractors.why_tempting: Washing dirty fruit sounds as if it ought to remove something, even if the wine tastes the same.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the washed fruit held less of the smoke compounds. It says that the washing “made no difference”, and one washed lot even read a little higher than its neighbour (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: A higher reading on washed fruit is strange, so it seems natural that Pemberdine would explain it.
distractors.why_wrong: Pemberdine draws no conclusion from it: Pemberdine “will not build on a single pair”, that is, on one comparison. The text gives no cause for the higher reading and never mentions ash blown back (step 3).

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “What are we told about …” questions, find the sentences about the named thing and check each part of the option against them. Here the result has two parts, and B keeps both.
p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A time from elsewhere in the text can be attached to the wrong claim. “A day or two” belongs to the locking of the smoke inside the grape, not to hosing.

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The text says: “Leaves take the phenols up too, but what a leaf takes up stays in the leaf.” D says the same. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the leaves of the vines, so the answer must be stated in the text. Leaves come up near the end of the second paragraph.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “Leaves take the phenols up too, but what a leaf takes up stays in the leaf.” The phenols are the smoke compounds described at the start of the paragraph.

steps.title: Read the whole sentence
steps.text: The first half says that leaves absorb the phenols. The second half, after “but”, says that the phenols go no further: they stay in the leaf.

steps.title: See why the district picks by hand
steps.text: Leaves matter “only when they reach the fermenter with the grapes, which is why the district picks by hand after a fire”. The fermenter is the tank where the juice becomes wine.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches the sentence. A completes it the wrong way, B adds something that the text never says, and C changes the picking by hand into stripping the leaves.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Leaves take up the phenols and keep them. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence begins by saying that leaves take the phenols up, and a reader who stops at the comma may expect them to pass the phenols on.
distractors.why_wrong: The sentence goes on: “what a leaf takes up stays in the leaf” (step 3). The phenols in a leaf do not travel on to the bunches.

distractors.why_tempting: Drying leaves could plausibly give off what they have absorbed, so B sounds like real science.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions leaves drying or giving anything off. It says that what a leaf takes up “stays in the leaf” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does say that something is done about leaves at harvest after a fire.
distractors.why_wrong: What the text describes is picking by hand, so that leaves do not reach the fermenter with the grapes (step 4). It never says that leaves are stripped off the vines.

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: Read a sentence to its end. A “but” in the middle often changes what the first half seems to say, and the right option follows the whole sentence.
p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: A gives the natural guess about leaves – that they pass the smoke on – which is exactly what the second half of the sentence rules out.

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The ashy smell is set free in the mouth, by “Enzymes in saliva, and the bacteria alongside them”, and the same six tasters mark it harder year after year. So part of the ashy finish is made in each taster’s own mouth, which is C. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that the answer is not stated outright; here you must join the explanation of the ashy taste with the disagreement in the panel.

steps.title: Find the explanation
steps.text: Quennerly describes January wines that “gave the nose very little and then turned dry and ashy half a minute after they were swallowed”. Then the text explains: “The sugar comes off in the mouth. Enzymes in saliva, and the bacteria alongside them, cut the phenol loose, and it reaches the nose from behind, after the glass has been put down.”

steps.title: Find the disagreement
steps.text: “Her panel does not agree with itself about how much of it there is. Six of the twenty-four mark the ashy finish harder than the rest, year after year; one tasted the worst lot of the vintage and called it clean.”

steps.title: Join the two
steps.text: The smoke compound is set free by each taster’s own saliva and bacteria, and the differences between the tasters are steady: the same six mark harder “year after year”. That points to something in the tasters, not only in the wine. So part of what each taster meets is made in that taster’s mouth, not in the glass.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C joins the two facts. A puts the difference in smelling smoke in the air, B says that every trained taster finds the ashy finish, and D says that the panel cannot be trusted, while the writer agrees that the panel’s median should win.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The ashy finish is partly made in the taster’s mouth. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Some people do notice smells more than others, so the six could simply have sharper noses.
distractors.why_wrong: The wines Quennerly describes “gave the nose very little”. The ashy smell reaches the nose “from behind, after the glass has been put down” (step 2), once saliva has set it free; the text never says that the six are more sensitive to smoke in the air.

distractors.why_tempting: A tasting panel sounds expert, so it seems that an ashy finish that is really in the wine should be there for every taster on the panel to find.
distractors.why_wrong: One taster on the panel “tasted the worst lot of the vintage and called it clean” (step 3), so even a panel taster does not always find it. And the ashy smell is set free in the mouth (step 2), so it does not belong to the wine alone.

distractors.why_tempting: A panel that disagrees with itself can look unreliable, and laboratory numbers look exact.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite. Quennerly calls the panel’s median “the only figure that has ever predicted what a drinker will say”, and the writer agrees: “She is right about that.” Quennerly is “untroubled by the spread”; the disagreement is not used against the panel.

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: For “implied” questions, join a mechanism with an observation. Here the mechanism (the smell is set free in the mouth) explains the observation (the tasters disagree in a steady way).
p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: A disagreement inside a panel tempts you to distrust the panel, as D does. But Quennerly is “untroubled by the spread”, and the writer still backs the median.

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Quennerly says that a reading which contradicts the panel’s median “should give way”, and the writer adds: “She is right about that.” The writer backs the panel without any hedge, which is A. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s own attitude to the laboratory readings. Keep the writer apart from Pemberdine and Quennerly, and look for sentences in which the writer judges.

steps.title: Find Quennerly’s claim
steps.text: Quennerly says: “The median is the only figure that has ever predicted what a drinker will say … and a reading that contradicts it should give way.” The median is the panel’s middle score, and a reading is a laboratory measurement.

steps.title: Find the writer’s verdict
steps.text: The next sentences are the writer’s: “She is right about that. The January readings were unremarkable and the January wines were not.” The writer agrees without any hedge and adds the evidence: the readings showed nothing special, yet the wines turned ashy.

steps.title: Find more of the writer’s voice
steps.text: Elsewhere the writer judges in the writer’s own voice too: “Thickness of smoke is no guide either.” And the small ferment tasted from a jar is “the sensible answer”, though “still too slow for a fire that comes in the last fortnight”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches the writer’s plain agreement. B gives the writer Pemberdine’s wish, C ignores “She is right about that”, and D calls the testing a waste, which the writer never does.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Where the panel and a reading disagree, the writer sides with the panel. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The last paragraph turns to the search for a threshold, and Pemberdine is the text’s main scientist.
distractors.why_wrong: The wish is Pemberdine’s: “Pemberdine wants a threshold a grower could act on sooner.” The writer never says that one will soon be found, and right after the wish, the writer reports Quennerly’s view that any threshold “will be wrong in both directions”.

distractors.why_tempting: In the last paragraph the writer does set Pemberdine’s and Quennerly’s views on a threshold side by side without choosing.
distractors.why_wrong: On the question asked here – a reading against the panel – the writer does choose: “She is right about that” (step 3). Leaving the reader to decide is not what that sentence does.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer shows that readings can mislead, so the testing might seem to be dismissed as a waste.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer never says that the growers would be better off without the testing. The nearest idea is Quennerly’s: Quennerly “would spend the money on more tasters” instead of on a threshold. The writer judges that a reading should give way to the panel where the two disagree (step 3), which is a different point, and reports the laboratory’s findings, such as “nine parts bound for every part free”, without doubting them.

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For attitude questions, look for a sentence in which the writer judges what someone else has said, such as “She is right about that.” Such a sentence shows the writer’s own position more clearly than any report.
p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Keep the voices apart. The wish for a threshold is Pemberdine’s, and the wish to spend the money on more tasters is Quennerly’s. The writer’s own position is in a sentence that judges a claim: “She is right about that.”

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: Every paragraph turns on the smoke compounds that the grape locks away with a sugar – “odourless, and unable to evaporate” – and on the trouble this causes growers. B names the hidden form and its cost. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the right answer must cover all its main parts, not just one paragraph.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1: washing the fruit made no difference, because “by then there was nothing on the outside of a berry left to wash off”. Paragraph 2: inside the grape, the smoke compounds are joined to a sugar and become “odourless, and unable to evaporate”. Paragraph 3: the locked smell is set free in the mouth, after the wine is swallowed, and that is “the awkward part for anyone judging affected fruit by nose”. Paragraph 4: other rules of thumb fail, and a wine can turn ashy after bottling. Paragraph 5: the slow test that the district now uses, and “Forty tonnes went on the ground in March, on a reading and a nervous buyer.”

steps.title: Find the thread
steps.text: One fact runs through every paragraph: the grape stores its smoke in a locked form that the nose cannot find. The rest is what that costs growers: wasted washing, misleading readings, slow tests and fruit thrown away.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B names both the locked form and its cost. A is only the opening trial, C is one clause about where the compounds come from, and D makes the text a story of losses and quarrels with buyers.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about grapes storing smoke where the nose cannot find it, and what that costs growers. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The hosing trial is the first and most vivid scene in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The trial fills only the first paragraph. It leads into the explanation of why washing could not work, which is what the rest of the text builds on (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: C uses real words from the text, such as phenols and lignin.
distractors.why_wrong: Where the phenols come from takes up one clause of the second paragraph: they are “set free when the lignin in the wood comes apart in the heat”. The text is about what happens to them in the grape, not how they are formed (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text ends with forty tonnes of fruit thrown away and a nervous buyer, which sounds like losses and arguments.
distractors.why_wrong: That is one sentence near the end. The text never describes an argument with a buyer, and most of it explains how the smoke hides in the grape and why that makes the fruit so hard to judge (step 3).

p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For main-idea questions, find the one fact that every paragraph depends on. Here each paragraph comes back to the smoke that the grape locks away.
p5-elf-b16-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Vivid scenes at the start and at the end, the hosing and the forty tonnes, are easy to remember, but each fills only part of the text.

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Something is second nature to you when you do it without thinking, because you have done it so often. The directions arrive “in one breath”, so naming a long-closed shop is second nature. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Naming a shop that shut before the asker was born is second ___.” The asker is the stranger who wants directions.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The sentence before shows how the directions are given: “the whole set arrives in one breath, and the person answering has moved off before the last turning is out of their mouth.” No thought is spent on them. English says that something is second nature to you when you do it without thinking.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: A juncture is a point in time, especially an important one, or a place where things join. A fixture is something fixed in place, a person or thing that is always there, or a sports match. Texture is how something feels, such as a surface. The sentence is about how automatically people name the old shops, and second nature is the expression for that, so “nature” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Naming a shop that shut before the asker was born is second nature.” The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Directions are full of turnings and junctions, and “juncture” looks like junction.
distractors.why_wrong: A juncture is a point in time or a joining point. The sentence is about how naturally the old names come, and second nature is the expression for that (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: An old shop that everyone still steers by is like a fixture of the town, so the word feels apt.
distractors.why_wrong: The sentence is about the act of naming, not about the shop: the naming comes without thought. That is what second nature means (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Texture” ends in -ture like the key and can describe the feel of a place.
distractors.why_wrong: Texture is how something feels, a surface or even a place. The sentence is about doing something without thinking, not about how anything feels, and second nature is the expression for that (step 2).

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap follows a word such as “second”, think of fixed expressions that begin with it. Then check that the expression’s meaning fits the sentences around it.
p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: All four nouns end in -ture, and “fixture” fits the topic of old shops. Choose the word that completes the expression, not the one that matches the topic.

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: Something travels badly when it loses its quality once it is moved somewhere else. The next sentence says that the directions, passed to a second stranger, “keep their shape and lose their meaning”. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Directions built like this ___ badly.” They are built from the points where the speaker has turned for years, so the route comes out in the right order while “the names on it stay private”.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The next sentence explains the gap: “Passed to a second stranger, they keep their shape and lose their meaning.” English often says that a wine, a joke or an idea travels badly when it does not keep its quality away from where it began. That is what happens to these directions.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To commute is usually to travel regularly between home and work. To journey is a formal way to say to make a trip, usually a long one. To migrate is usually to move to live somewhere else, as birds or people do, or to move data to a new system. All three are about moving, but the sentence needs the sense of keeping or losing quality when something is passed on, and travel well or badly is the common way to say that. So “travel” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Directions built like this travel badly.” The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage is about routes through a town, and commuting is everyday travel.
distractors.why_wrong: To commute is usually to travel regularly between home and work. The sentence is about whether the directions keep their meaning when passed on, which is what travel badly says (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Journey” is the closest in meaning to “travel”, since both are about going from place to place.
distractors.why_wrong: As a verb, journey usually means to make a long trip. The sentence needs the sense of losing quality when passed on, and the common expression for that is to travel badly (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Migrating is moving from one place to another, which suits directions being passed on.
distractors.why_wrong: To migrate is usually to move to live somewhere else, or to move data to a new system. The sentence needs the common way to say that something loses its quality when passed on – the directions “keep their shape and lose their meaning” – and that is travel badly (step 2).

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a gap is followed by an adverb such as “badly”, ask which verb forms a common expression with it, and then check the expression against the next sentence.
p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: All four verbs are about moving, which matches the topic of directions. The next sentence, not the topic, shows which one the frame needs.

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The town “will take being wrong over being thought cold”, so a shrug must be heard as something cold and unfriendly. Unfriendliness towards someone is hostility. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Here, though, a shrug is heard as ___, and the town will take being wrong over being thought cold.” A shrug is a lift of the shoulders that shows you do not know or do not care.

steps.title: Use the clue after the gap
steps.text: The second half of the sentence says what the town fears: being thought cold, that is, unfriendly. So a shrug in place of directions is heard as unfriendliness, and the town would rather give a wrong answer. Hostility is unfriendliness, being against someone.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: Docility is being quiet and easy to control. Futility is pointlessness. Civility is politeness. Docility and futility say nothing about seeming cold, and civility points the other way: a town would not choose being wrong to avoid seeming polite. So “hostility” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Here, though, a shrug is heard as hostility.” The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Docility” has the same -ility ending and sounds like a word about manners.
distractors.why_wrong: Docility is being quiet and easy to control. Here a shrug is not heard as obedience: the sentence ties it to “being thought cold” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph has just counted wasted time – twenty minutes and a wrong turning – so pointlessness is in the air.
distractors.why_wrong: The gap names what a shrug is taken for, and the second half of the sentence shows that it would make the town seem cold. Futility, pointlessness, is not a cold attitude towards a person (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Civility” belongs to the same field of manners as the passage, and a shrug can seem politely modest.
distractors.why_wrong: Civility is politeness. The clause after the gap names what the town fears, being thought cold, and a town would not choose being wrong to avoid being thought polite (step 2).

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: Use the clause after the gap: here “being thought cold” tells you that the gap names something unfriendly.
p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Several options belong to the field of manners. Decide first whether the gap is positive or negative, then choose.

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The town would rather be wrong than seem cold, and so an answer is always given, at once. The second sentence is a result of the first, and “Consequently” means as a result. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, an answer is always produced, and it comes at the speed of a reflex.” A reflex is a reaction that happens without thought.

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The sentence before ends: “the town will take being wrong over being thought cold.” Because people fear seeming cold, they always produce an answer, and at once. The gapped sentence is the result of that fear, so the gap needs a result word: “Consequently”, meaning as a result.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Conceivably” means possibly. “Conversely” means the other way round. “Concurrently” means at the same time. The gapped sentence is not a guess – the writer reports the habit as plain fact from the first paragraph on – and it neither reverses the sentence before nor runs beside it. So “Consequently” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Consequently, an answer is always produced.” The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: “Conceivably” sounds careful, and careful words can feel safe.
distractors.why_wrong: It would make the sentence a mere possibility, but the writer is not guessing: the first paragraph already reports the habit as plain fact – “Ask anyone … and you will be sent past the old brewery”. The sentence is a result of the town’s fear of seeming cold (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Conversely” is a formal link that, like the key, begins with Con-.
distractors.why_wrong: “Conversely” introduces the opposite of what came before. Always producing an answer is not the opposite of fearing to seem cold; it is its result (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The answer comes at once, so a word about time can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: “Concurrently” means at the same time as something else. The sentence does not describe two things happening together; it says what follows from the town’s fear (step 2).

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: For a connective gap, ask how the gapped sentence relates to the one before: a result, a contrast, a guess, or something happening at the same time.
p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: All four options begin with Con-, so their shape gives nothing away. Decide the relationship first.

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: To take something in your stride is to deal with it calmly. The sentence sets most visitors against the few who “go home with something to say about the place”, so most of them take it calmly. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Most visitors take all this in their ___; a few go home with something to say about the place.”

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The semicolon sets most visitors against a few. The few go home with something to say about the place, most likely a complaint. So the many must react calmly. English says that you take something in your stride when you deal with it calmly, without letting it upset you.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: Gait is the way someone walks. Pace is usually speed, often walking speed. A step is one movement of the foot. All three are about walking, like stride, but the sentence is about how calmly visitors react, and take something in your stride is the expression for that. So “stride” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Most visitors take all this in their stride.” The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Gait” is a precise word for a way of walking, and the passage is about walking routes.
distractors.why_wrong: Gait is the way someone walks. The sentence is about how visitors react, and the expression for reacting calmly is to take something in your stride (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: People speak of doing things at their own pace, so a pace of their own sounds familiar.
distractors.why_wrong: Pace usually means speed. The sentence is not about how fast visitors do anything but about how calmly they react, which is what take something in your stride says (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Being in step is a familiar phrase, and step is a walking word like stride.
distractors.why_wrong: A step is one movement of the foot, and being in step means moving together with others. The sentence needs the expression for reacting calmly: take something in your stride (step 2).

p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: In idiom gaps, read the whole frame – here “take all this in their ___” – and the clause after it, which shows the meaning the idiom must have.
p5-elf-b16-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: All four nouns are about walking, which matches the passage. The topic makes each one feel right; the expression decides.

p5-elf-b16-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: “While the wind is still on the wall, it pushes in at those same joints, and the tray holds what it has collected.” So before the wind drops, the water stays on the tray because the wind presses in. That is D. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what is said about the open joints before the wind drops, that is, while the wind is still blowing. The answer must be stated in the text. The open joints are gaps between the bricks above a window, deliberately left without mortar.

steps.title: Follow the water
steps.text: In a long south-westerly, a wind from the south-west, the outer brick “wets through”. The water that gets past it “runs down into the cavity, onto a tray bedded in over the opening, which discharges it through the open joints.” The cavity is the space inside the wall, and to discharge water is to let it out.

steps.title: Find what happens while the wind blows
steps.text: “While the wind is still on the wall, it pushes in at those same joints, and the tray holds what it has collected. In the lull, the tray lets go.” A lull is a short calm. So while the wind blows, the wind presses inwards and the water waits on the tray.

steps.title: See what comes later
steps.text: In the lull the tray lets go, but “Not all of the joints run, and none for long.” The head is the top of the window opening. A head that gives back nothing an hour after the wind drops “is worth recording”, but an open joint cannot tell you why. A stop end is the closed end of the tray.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches the sentence. A has the wind forcing the water out, B says that little water has reached the tray, and C adds a fault that the text links to a later moment.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Before the wind drops, the tray keeps its water because the wind presses in at the joints. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A strong wind on a wall with holes in it sounds as if it would drive the water out.
distractors.why_wrong: The wind works the other way: it “pushes in at those same joints”, and the tray holds its water (step 3). And even in the lull, “Not all of the joints run” (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: The first part fits the start of the process: the rain does wet the outer brick.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that little water has reached the tray, and B says nothing about the joints, which the question asks about. What the text says about this moment is that the wind “pushes in at those same joints” and the tray “holds what it has collected” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Its first half is right: nothing comes out while the wind blows, and a missing stop end is mentioned in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The text gives the wind as the reason why nothing comes out (step 3). A head is worth recording if it “gives back nothing an hour after the wind drops”, and even then “an open joint cannot say” whether the tray is blocked or is spilling past a missing stop end (step 4).

p5-elf-b16-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: Watch the time words. Here “While the wind is still on the wall”, “In the lull” and “an hour after the wind drops” mark three different moments, and the question asks about the first.
p5-elf-b16-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: C starts with a true statement and then adds a wrong cause. Check every part of a two-part option, not just the first.

p5-elf-b16-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The keep was charged by the night, and the only notice was the Sunday crying. A heifer taken up on a Monday cost four shillings and one taken up on the Saturday one and sixpence, though both were fetched on the Sunday they were cried, so the bill turned on the day of the week. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that the answer is not stated outright; here you must join the charges, the rule for notice and the two bills.

steps.title: Find the charges
steps.text: The table charged “a shilling for taking up a beast and sixpence a night for its keep”. To take up a beast is to catch it and shut it in the pound, a walled pen for straying animals.

steps.title: Find the notice
steps.text: “Skellorne was to cry what he held at the church door each Sunday after service, and nowhere else.” To cry here means to announce aloud. And “Farmers on the far side of the common heard of a beast no other way.” So owners on the far side of the common learned of a beast only on a Sunday.

steps.title: Check the two bills
steps.text: Twelve pence made a shilling, and a heifer is a young cow. The Monday heifer stayed six nights before the Sunday: one shilling plus six sixpences, which is four shillings. The Saturday heifer stayed one night: one shilling plus sixpence, one and sixpence. “Both were fetched on the Sunday they were cried”, so the owners acted alike, and the difference in the bills came from the day of capture.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B follows from the three facts. A gives the fees to the parish, C blames slow owners, and D gives Skellorne a choice that the text never gives: the crying was fixed for Sunday.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: What an owner paid depended on which day of the week the beast was taken up. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Fees were paid on every beast, so the pound looks like a source of money, and “probably” makes the claim modest.
distractors.why_wrong: The fees did not go to the parish: “The pinder's office carried no wage: Jabez Skellorne had the fees instead”. The pinder was the keeper of the pound, and the text mentions no money going to the parish.

distractors.why_tempting: Its first half is true: the table did charge by the night, so a long stay meant a big bill.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing shows a slow owner. Owners on the far side of the common heard of a beast only at the Sunday crying, and both owners fetched their heifers “on the Sunday they were cried” (steps 3 and 4). The heavier bill came from the day the heifer was taken up.

distractors.why_tempting: The fees were Skellorne’s, so a longer stay did pay better, and it is tempting to give Skellorne the decision too.
distractors.why_wrong: The text gives Skellorne a fixed duty instead: Skellorne “was to cry what he held at the church door each Sunday after service, and nowhere else” (step 3). A beast was kept until its owner came for it, and the notice was fixed for Sunday, so the length of a stay depended on the owner and on that fixed day, not on Skellorne’s choice.

p5-elf-b16-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a text gives two worked cases, ask what was the same and what was different. Here the owners acted alike, so the difference in the bills must come from the day each beast was taken up.
p5-elf-b16-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: C and D each join something true – the nightly charge, the fees that a longer stay brought Skellorne – to a claim that the text does not support. In D the unsupported claim comes first. Check every part of the option.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Moving a flight two thousand feet down is cheap – “The maneuver is the cheap part” – but showing that it worked is hard, because the wet layers cannot be seen and an empty satellite picture can mean several things. B names both. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the right answer must fit the text as a whole, not just one paragraph. A contrail is the white line of ice that an aircraft leaves in the sky.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 explains why some contrails last: by the time a contrail is an hour old, most of its ice came “out of the air the airplane was passing through”. Paragraph 2 says that the wet layers cannot be seen and are hard to forecast. Paragraph 3 describes the change: flights planned “two thousand feet beneath” a forecast layer, at night. Paragraph 4 gives the audit: most planned step-downs were never flown, and the change costs little fuel. Paragraph 5 explains why the satellite pictures cannot show that the change worked.

steps.title: Name both halves
steps.text: The change of height is cheap: an adjusted aircraft burned “about two percent more”, and Colverdine calls the move the cheap part. The hard part is proving that it worked: “a success looks like an empty picture”, and so do three other cases. The right answer must name both.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B names both halves. A is one thread that runs through the text, C is the science of paragraph 1, and D compares two kinds of warming that the text never compares.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about a cheap change of height and the trouble of showing that it worked. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Humidity forecasts are a real problem in the text, and they sound technical and central.
distractors.why_wrong: Poor humidity forecasts come up more than once, but they are one thread, not the subject. A says nothing about the change of height, its small cost or the counting in paragraph 5 (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does explain in detail how ice crystals feed in wet air, so C names real content.
distractors.why_wrong: That explanation is the background in paragraph 1. The trial, the audit and the counting in paragraphs 3 to 5 are not about how crystals grow (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text says that a contrail “holds in heat”, and it mentions fuel, so a comparison of the two sounds possible.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never compares the warming from contrails with the warming from burning fuel. Fuel comes up only as the small cost of the change and as one reason why planned descents were not flown.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For main-idea questions, map the paragraphs and look for the contrast that ties them together. Here it is between a move that is cheap and a result that is hard to prove.
p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Detailed science at the start is often background. The first paragraph explains contrails; the text is about what was done and what can be shown.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: A layer can “make no cloud of its own”, so “the sky stays clear”, and it has “a depth that would fit inside a small hill”. A says that the layers are shallow and hold no cloud. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the layers themselves – the layers of wet air – so the answer must be stated in the text. They are described in paragraph 2.

steps.title: Find the cloud
steps.text: “Air can sit well past ice saturation and make no cloud of its own, because starting a crystal from nothing needs roughly half again as much vapor as keeping an existing one alive.” Past ice saturation means holding more water vapour than ice can hold. So the layers hold no cloud: “the sky stays clear”.

steps.title: Find the depth
steps.text: The layer “runs a couple of hundred miles with a depth that would fit inside a small hill”. Vestrigg adds: “The layers are usually shallow enough that one step down is out of them.” So they are shallow.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A gives both facts. B brings in cirrus, which the text never mentions, C says that the layers can be seen, and D gives the layers what the contrails do.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The layers are shallow and hold no cloud of their own. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Contrails and cirrus, thin high cloud, are both made of ice, so wet air and cirrus seem to belong together.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: the layer makes “no cloud of its own”, and “the sky stays clear” (step 2). Cirrus is never mentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: Pilots can see weather ahead, so a layer of wet air sounds like something they could spot.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that “a layer like that has nothing in it to look at”, and that “the first anyone knows of it is the mark an airplane leaves crossing it”.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does talk about something spreading after an aircraft passes.
distractors.why_wrong: What spreads is the contrail: “a spreading contrail”, which needs time “to spread wide enough for a satellite to register it”. The text never says that the layer spreads.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: For “What are we told about …” questions, find every sentence about the named thing. Here the layers are described in paragraph 2, and Vestrigg adds one fact in paragraph 3.
p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: A verb from one part of the text can be attached to the wrong noun. The contrail spreads; the text never says that the layer does.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: By day a contrail holds in heat but also “turns some sunlight back toward space”, so the two effects pull against each other; “after dark there is nothing pulling the other way”. D says this. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the decision to move only night flights. Look for the sentence that gives the reason for “Nights only”.

steps.title: Find the reason
steps.text: “Nights only: a spreading contrail holds in heat that would otherwise leave, and in daylight it also turns some sunlight back toward space, so the two effects pull against one another, while after dark there is nothing pulling the other way.”

steps.title: Read the two effects
steps.text: One effect warms: the contrail holds in heat. The other pulls the opposite way, but only in daylight: the contrail turns some sunlight back towards space. By day the two pull against each other. At night there is no sunlight to turn back, so only the warming is left. That is why only night flights were moved.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D gives the reason. A brings in a reason about traffic, B a difference in depth, and C says that a daylight contrail cools overall, which the text never says.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: After dark nothing works against the warming, because there is no sunlight to turn away. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Light traffic at night sounds like a practical reason for moving flights then.
distractors.why_wrong: The text gives a different reason, the two effects of a contrail (step 2). It never says that traffic is light at night, and it never gives traffic as a reason for “Nights only”.

distractors.why_tempting: The forecast layers are central to the decision, and night is when the flights were moved.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never compares layers found by night with layers found by day, and it gives no depth that changes with the time of day. The reason it gives for “Nights only” is the two effects of a contrail (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: By day the contrail does turn some sunlight back towards space, which sounds like cooling.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says only that by day “the two effects pull against one another” (step 2). It never says which one wins, so it never says that a daylight contrail cools the ground instead of warming it.
