p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question asks about a decision, find the sentence that gives its reason and read every part of it. Here “in daylight” and “after dark” set up the contrast.
p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: C turns two effects that “pull against one another” into a winner. When a text says that two things work against each other but not which one wins, do not choose an option that names a winner.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Of 141 flights left to fly through a forecast layer, only 61 “left a mark anybody could find afterward”, and the forecast “was calling for wet air a good deal more often than the sky supplied it”. The step-downs were planned on the same forecast, so many of the descents that were flown will have taken aircraft out of air where they would have left no lasting mark anyway. That is C. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that the answer is not stated outright; here you must use the flights that were left alone to judge the forecast, and then apply that to the flights that were moved.

steps.title: Find the flights left alone
steps.text: “Of 141 flights that were left alone and flew straight through a forecast layer, 61 left a mark anybody could find afterward.” These flights were not moved, so they show what happened in the air that the forecast had called wet.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.text: Fewer than half left a mark that anyone could find afterwards, and the next sentence draws the lesson: “The forecast was calling for wet air a good deal more often than the sky supplied it.” In other words, the forecast often called for a layer that was not really there.

steps.title: Apply it to the descents
steps.text: The descents were planned on the same forecast: “On nights when the forecast laid one of these layers across a route, the flight was planned two thousand feet beneath it”. And “Of 406 plans written with the step-down in them, 96 were flown that way”. If the forecast often called for wet air that was not there, many of those 96 aircraft stepped down out of air where they would have left no lasting mark anyway. The writer adds a caution: this is “the best of those readings”, not a count, which is why C says “many” and “will have”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C draws the one-step consequence. A moves “fewer than half” to the wrong fact, B reverses the forecast’s error, and D says that no contrail could form, although 61 flights left one.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Many of the descents that were flown will have bought nothing. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Fewer than half” matches the numbers: 61 is fewer than half of 141.
distractors.why_wrong: Fewer than half of the flights left a mark that anyone could find afterwards, but every one of them “flew straight through a forecast layer” (step 2). A puts the fraction on the wrong thing.

distractors.why_tempting: The forecast clearly made mistakes, and missing real layers is one kind of mistake.
distractors.why_wrong: The text reports the other kind: the forecast called for wet air “a good deal more often than the sky supplied it” (step 3). And these flights could not show a missed layer, since every one of them flew through a layer that the forecast had called.

distractors.why_tempting: Many of the flights left no mark that anyone could find afterwards, so it can seem that contrails could not form where they flew.
distractors.why_wrong: Sixty-one of them “left a mark anybody could find afterward” (step 2), so contrails did form at those heights.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “implied” questions about a comparison, use the group that was left alone to judge the forecast, and then ask what that means for the group that was changed.
p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Numbers are easy to attach to the wrong thing. Check what each number counts: 141 flights through forecast layers, 61 of them leaving a mark that anyone could find afterwards, 96 descents flown.

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer calls the satellite count “the smallest thing those two winters produced” and says that one lasting finding “comes off records the center already keeps and needed no picture at all”. The count settled less than the records did, which is A. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s own attitude to the satellite count, not Vestrigg’s or Colverdine’s. The writer’s own voice is clearest at the end of paragraph 5.

steps.title: Find the writer’s ranking
steps.text: “But the satellite count is the smallest thing those two winters produced. Colverdine is right about the cheap part, and the findings that will outlast the trial are his: that the forecast asks for more descents than the sky calls for, and that most of the descents it asks for are never flown.”

steps.title: Compare the two sources
steps.text: Then: “The second of those comes off records the center already keeps and needed no picture at all.” The finding that most planned descents are never flown came from the centre’s own records. A picture, the writer says, settles a flight only when it shows a contrail: “An empty one settles nothing”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches the ranking. B gives the writer Vestrigg’s hope, C ignores the ranking, and D goes further than the writer, who grants that a picture showing a contrail settles that flight.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer thinks that the satellite count settled less than the centre’s own records. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The sensors are the last hopeful idea in the text, and they would measure what the pictures cannot.
distractors.why_wrong: That hope is Vestrigg’s: Vestrigg “believes the rest would follow”. The writer’s only answer is “Perhaps it would”, and the text ends: “The sensors have not been fitted.”

distractors.why_tempting: The text gives a long, fair account of what the pictures can and cannot show, which can sound neutral.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer does prefer one kind of evidence: the count is “the smallest thing those two winters produced”, while a finding from the records “needed no picture at all” (steps 2 and 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer explains at length why an empty picture proves nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer grants that “A picture that shows a contrail settles that one flight”, and never asks for the counting to stop. Ranking the count low is not calling it worthless (step 3).

p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, look for the writer’s ranking words, such as “the smallest thing” and “will outlast”. They show which evidence the writer values more.
p5-elf-b17-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: The last forward-looking idea in a text is not always the writer’s. The sensors are Vestrigg’s hope; the writer says only “Perhaps it would”.

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: An umbrella is worth less than the fare back to collect it, so few owners will come for one, and it is no surprise that the umbrella rack is cleared more often than the rest of the room. “Predictably” means as you would expect. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, the umbrella rack is cleared twice a year and the rest of the room once.”

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The sentence before says: “An umbrella is worth less than the fare back into town to collect it, and anyone who has left one on the number 14 works that out somewhere around the second stop.” So umbrellas are left uncollected and their rack fills up, and it is cleared twice as often as the rest of the room. That follows just as you would expect, so the gap needs “Predictably”.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Ostensibly” means apparently, but perhaps not really. “Arguably” marks a claim that could be argued about. “Conversely” brings in the opposite. The clearing is a plain fact that follows from the umbrella’s low value: nothing hints that it only seems to happen, it is not a matter of opinion, and it is not the opposite of what came before. So “Predictably” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Predictably, the umbrella rack is cleared twice a year and the rest of the room once.” The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Ostensibly” sounds formal and fits the start of a sentence about an office routine.
distractors.why_wrong: “Ostensibly” suggests that something only seems to be so. Nothing in the text casts doubt on the clearing; it follows from the umbrellas being left behind (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Arguably” sounds careful, and careful words can feel safe.
distractors.why_wrong: “Arguably” marks a claim that is open to debate. How often a rack is cleared is a plain fact, and it follows from what the sentence before says about umbrellas (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence before talks about something being worth less, which can feel like the set-up for a contrast.
distractors.why_wrong: “Conversely” brings in the opposite of what came before. Clearing the umbrella rack more often is not the opposite of umbrellas being left behind; it is the result you would expect (step 2).

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: For a connective gap, decide how the gapped sentence relates to the one before. When it is the result you would expect, a word like “Predictably” fits.
p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Careful-sounding words such as “Arguably” are not always right. Here the sentence states a fact, so a word that hedges it does not fit.

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: To give something up for lost is to stop expecting to get it back. By the time the tag is filled in, the owner has usually done exactly that. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “By the time that tag is filled in, the owner has usually ___ it up for lost.” The tag is the paper label that every item gets.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The frame has the pattern “___ it up for lost”. English says that you give something up for lost when you stop hoping to see it again. That fits the sentence: by the time an item reaches the office and its tag is filled in, the owner has usually stopped hoping.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To write something up usually means to write a report on it, as in writing up notes. To count something up is to add it up. To put something up for something is usually to offer it, as in putting a house up for sale. The sentence is about an owner who has stopped hoping, and give something up for lost is the expression for that, so “given” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The owner has usually given it up for lost.” The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Writing something off means accepting that it is lost, so “written” feels close to the meaning.
distractors.why_wrong: Writing something off is close in meaning, but the frame has up for lost, and to write something up usually means to write a report on it. The owner has stopped hoping, and the expression for that is to give something up for lost (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: You can count something as lost, so “counted” seems to fit the idea.
distractors.why_wrong: Counting something as lost is close in meaning, but the frame has up for lost, and to count something up is to add it up. The pattern of the frame belongs to give something up for lost (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: You can put something down as lost, and put up for is a familiar pattern.
distractors.why_wrong: To put something up for something is usually to offer it, as in putting a car up for sale. Nothing in the sentence is about offering the item; the owner has stopped hoping to get it back (step 2).

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When the frame contains a small word and a preposition, as in “___ it up for lost”, look for the verb that forms an expression with all of them.
p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Several options are close in meaning: you can write something off, count it as lost or put it down as lost. But the frame’s pattern, up for lost, belongs to give something up for lost.

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: To take someone at their word is to believe what they say without asking for proof. Nobody is asked for a receipt; a matching description is enough. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Whoever turns up describes the thing, and if the description matches the tag, the office takes them at their ___ and the coat goes back across the counter.”

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The sentence before says: “No one is asked for a receipt or a crime number.” The office asks for no proof and simply believes the description. English says that you take someone at their word when you believe what they say without proof.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: Honour is being honest and keeping your promises. Face recalls the expression take something at face value, to accept it as it looks, but that expression needs value after face, and the frame has no room for it. Trust is close too: to take something on trust is to believe it without proof, but that expression has on, while the frame has at. The frame “takes them at their ___” matches take someone at their word, so “word” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The office takes them at their word.” The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Honour belongs to the same field of trust and honesty, and people give their word of honour.
distractors.why_wrong: Honour belongs to the same field, but the frame “takes them at their ___” belongs to take someone at their word (step 2). Honour comes in other patterns, such as on their honour.

distractors.why_tempting: To take something at face value means to accept it as it looks, which is close to what the office does.
distractors.why_wrong: That expression needs value after face, and the frame ends with their ___. Believing a person’s description without proof is taking them at their word (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The whole paragraph is about trusting people, so “trust” fits the theme.
distractors.why_wrong: To take something on trust is close in meaning, but that expression has on, while the frame has at their. The expression that matches the frame is to take someone at their word (step 2).

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a gap ends a pattern such as “takes them at their ___”, think of expressions with exactly those words, and check the meaning against the sentence before.
p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Three options are close in meaning or theme: honour, face and trust. Decide by the pattern of the frame as well as by the meaning.

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: “Everywhere else in the room a description is enough. At the drawer it is not”, so the questions there must be harder and more careful. Searching questions try hard to find out the truth. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “At the drawer it is not, and the questions asked there are ___.” The drawer is the locked one under the counter.

steps.title: Follow the contrast
steps.text: Everywhere else a description is enough, and “Two questions is the usual limit”. At the drawer a description is not enough, because the drawer holds anything “worth more than about fifty pounds”, such as a laptop or a passport. So the questions there must be the opposite of easy: careful questions that try to find out the truth. Such questions are called searching.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: Obliging means helpful and willing. Reassuring means making someone feel less worried. Forgiving means ready to excuse, or not strict. All three describe the easy side, but “At the drawer it is not” sets the drawer against the easy room, so the gap needs a strict word: “searching”.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The questions asked there are searching.” The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The office is helpful everywhere else, so a helpful word seems to suit it.
distractors.why_wrong: Obliging means helpful and willing. The sentence sets the drawer against the easy rule of the room, so the questions there are stricter, not more helpful (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A worried owner might want to be reassured when claiming something valuable.
distractors.why_wrong: Reassuring questions would calm the claimant. The questions at the drawer are there to test the claim, since “a description is enough” everywhere else but not at the drawer (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The room is relaxed about claims, so a gentle word seems to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Forgiving means ready to excuse, or not strict – which describes the rest of the room. The gap describes the drawer, where a description is not enough (step 2).

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a sentence says “it is not”, the gap often names the opposite of what was true before. Find what was true before, then choose its opposite.
p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Three options are friendly words that match the relaxed room. The contrast with the room calls for the one strict word.

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: A foregone conclusion is a result that is certain before it happens. The umbrella’s fate is settled “before the ink is dry”, while “a set of keys is another matter”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “An umbrella’s future is a foregone ___ before the ink is dry; a set of keys is another matter.” The ink is the writing on the item’s tag.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The umbrella’s end is certain from the moment it arrives: when its time is up, it goes into a bin bag. English calls a result that is certain from the start a foregone conclusion. Keys, by contrast, are kept in a tin past the ninety days.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: A resolution is a firm decision or the solving of a problem. A decision is a choice that someone makes. A conviction is a firm belief, or a court’s finding that someone is guilty. All are outcomes of a kind, but the sentence says that the umbrella’s future is certain in advance, which is what a foregone conclusion means. So “conclusion” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “An umbrella’s future is a foregone conclusion before the ink is dry.” The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A resolution is an outcome, and the sentence is about how things will turn out.
distractors.why_wrong: A resolution is a firm decision or the solving of a problem. The sentence says that the umbrella’s future is certain from the start, and the expression for that is a foregone conclusion (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The office does decide what happens to each item, so “decision” seems natural.
distractors.why_wrong: A decision is a choice that someone makes. The sentence is about a result that is certain from the start, and the expression for that is a foregone conclusion (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A conviction is a firm belief, and the office seems sure about umbrellas.
distractors.why_wrong: A conviction is a firm belief or a court’s finding of guilt. The sentence is not about anyone’s belief or a court case: it is about a result that is certain from the start, which is a foregone conclusion (step 2).

p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: Some adjectives are used mostly in one fixed expression. When you see a word like “foregone”, recall the expression it usually comes in.
p5-elf-b17-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: All four nouns end in -ion and name outcomes, so meaning alone does not decide. The expression does.

p5-elf-b17-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: “The pin is not fastened down.” Because nothing down there is fixed against a sideways push, the water moves the leaf a little and “beds its heel into the iron plate that lines the recess”. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the pin that the leaf stands on, so the answer must be stated in the text. A leaf is one of the pair of lock gates that meet in a V.

steps.title: Find the pin
steps.text: “Each leaf pivots on a heel post rounded by hand, and the post stands on a pin in a cup set in the stone. The pin is not fastened down.”

steps.title: Find what follows
steps.text: “Nothing down there is fixed against a sideways push, so the water shifts the leaf what little it can and beds its heel into the iron plate that lines the recess.” The heel is the end of the leaf at the wall, and the recess is the hollow in the wall where it sits. Because the pin is free, the leaf can settle firmly against the iron in the wall.

steps.title: See where the push goes
steps.text: “The push runs along the leaf into the masonry, and next to none of it reaches the pin. What the pin carries is the weight of the leaf.” Masonry is stonework. The collar at the top of the post is shimmed too, packed with thin pieces, but the text gives that a reason of its own: “that is a matter of hang, of the mitre posts meeting true”, that is, of the two leaves meeting properly.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches the text. B says that the pin is fixed hard, C gives the shimming of the collar the wrong reason, and D gives the pin the whole push.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The pin is not anchored, so the leaf can settle its heel against the iron in the wall. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: A gate holding back a canal sounds as if it should be fixed down as hard as possible.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “The pin is not fastened down”, and the water “shifts the leaf what little it can” (steps 2 and 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Its first half is true: the pin carries the weight of the leaf.
distractors.why_wrong: The second half gives the shimming the wrong reason. The text says that the collar’s shimming “is a matter of hang, of the mitre posts meeting true” (step 4). It never links the shimming to the weight on the pin, usually or otherwise.

distractors.why_tempting: The water presses hard on a lock gate, and the pin is at its foot, so it seems to take the force.
distractors.why_wrong: The push “runs along the leaf into the masonry, and next to none of it reaches the pin” (step 4). And the only hang the text mentions is a matter “of the mitre posts meeting true”, not of sending the push to the pin.

p5-elf-b17-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “What are we told about …” questions, read the sentence about the named thing and the one or two after it. Here the sentences after “The pin is not fastened down” explain why that matters.
p5-elf-b17-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Common sense says that a hinge should be fixed firmly. The text describes the opposite, so answer from the text, not from what seems sensible.

p5-elf-b17-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The one clause that protected a buyer covered only “the first thirteen weeks”, and “Nothing in the bargain bound a customer”. So a house could still leave after thirteen weeks, and nothing then gave the buyer money back. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Concluded” means that the answer follows from what the text states, although the text does not say it outright. Here you must read where the one protective rule stops.

steps.title: Find the rule
steps.text: “One clause covered the first thirteen weeks: a customer who fell off the round inside that time was struck out of the reckoning, and the price came down by that customer's weeks of takings.” A round is a milkman’s list of houses, and takings are the money taken.

steps.title: Read where it stops
steps.text: “Nothing in the bargain bound a customer”: any house could turn the float, the milk cart, away at the gate and buy from someone else next morning. So a house could leave at any time, after the thirteen weeks too. The clause gave money back only for houses lost inside the thirteen weeks, and the text gives no other protection, so after that the loss of a house was the buyer’s alone.

steps.title: Check the worked case
steps.text: There were 20 shillings (s) in a pound and 12 pence (d) in a shilling. Hobbage paid £168 for houses taking £21 a week, which is eight weeks of takings. On average each of the 120 houses took 3s 6d a week, and eight weeks of that is £1 8s. Nine average houses come to nine times £1 8s, exactly the “£12 12s” that came back, which fits all nine having gone inside the thirteen weeks.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C follows from the clause and its limit. A prices the round by houses instead of takings, B builds the price on debts that stayed with the seller, and D says that competition kept milk cheap, although the dairy fixed the price.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: After the thirteen weeks, the buyer alone carried the loss of a house that left. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “A hundred and twenty houses” is the most striking figure in the text, and the plant really was valued on top.
distractors.why_wrong: The second half is true, but the first is not: “the round itself was reckoned in weeks of takings”, that is, by the money the houses paid, not by how many houses there were. Even a lost customer came off the price “by that customer's weeks of takings” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: It starts from a true fact – the plant was valued on its own – and “mainly” makes it sound measured.
distractors.why_wrong: The price did not turn on debts. The round was “reckoned in weeks of takings”, and “What the houses owed on the day of the change stayed the seller's to collect”, so the debts were not part of the sale at all.

distractors.why_tempting: Its first half is true: any house could switch to another roundsman the next morning.
distractors.why_wrong: The milk came “at the price the dairy fixed”, whoever brought it, so switching roundsmen did not change the price. The text says nothing about milk prices in the town being kept down.

p5-elf-b17-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: A conclusion puts stated facts together. When a text gives a rule with a limit, such as “the first thirteen weeks”, ask what holds outside that limit, and check that no other sentence changes it.
p5-elf-b17-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A, B and D each contain something true. Do not stop at the true part: check every part of an option against the text.

p5-elf-b18-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text says: “But mortar that touches timber passes damp to it, and whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens until they decayed along its line.” D says the same. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about torching, so the answer must be stated in the text. The text explains the word itself: lime mortar with horsehair, “pressed up against the backs of the tiles from inside”.

steps.title: Find its job
steps.text: “It went on after the tiles were hung, and it was there to stop the fine snow, dust and draughts that wind pushes up between the tiles. At that job it worked.” A draught is a current of cold air.

steps.title: Find the damage
steps.text: Then comes the turn: “But mortar that touches timber passes damp to it, and whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens until they decayed along its line.” Battens are the thin strips of wood that the tiles hang on, and to decay is to rot. So the mortar held the wet against the wood, and the wood rotted there.

steps.title: See how the tiles hang
steps.text: The tiles do not depend on the torching: “The tiles themselves hang from two small lugs at the head, the nibs, hooked over each batten, with often only every fourth course nailed as well.” A course is a row of tiles.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D restates the damage. A says that the timber usually stayed sound, B gives torching the job of holding the tiles, and C makes it weathertight in all weather.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Torching held the wet against the battens, and they rotted. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Torching did protect the loft from the fine snow, dust and draughts, and the last sentence talks about sheltering.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the timber usually stayed sound. Far from sheltering the battens, mortar “passes damp” to timber, and whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens “until they decayed along its line” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Many people think that mortar is what holds roof tiles in place.
distractors.why_wrong: Every tile hangs from its nibs, “hooked over each batten” (step 4), so the unnailed courses were already hanging before any torching “went on”. The text gives torching a different job: stopping the fine snow, dust and draughts (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text says that “At that job it worked”, so torching sounds like a full defence against the weather.
distractors.why_wrong: Its job was narrower: “the fine snow, dust and draughts that wind pushes up between the tiles” (step 2). Nor did it keep the wet out of the roof: whatever wet reached the torching “sat against the battens until they decayed along its line” (step 3).

p5-elf-b18-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: Watch for “But” after a success. Here, soon after “At that job it worked”, a sentence begins with “But”, and that sentence holds the answer.
p5-elf-b18-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Success at one job is not success at everything. Torching stopped the fine snow, dust and draughts, yet the wet it held against the battens rotted them.

p5-elf-b18-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Six pews in the middle aisle stood vacant in 1848 and four in 1849. In the plan of 1851, where ruled lines cut the boxes into single sittings, “the vacant marks are gone”. Put together, these facts point to B: letting seats singly filled pews that would not let whole. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Concluded” means that the answer follows from what the text states, although the text does not say it outright. Here the wardens’ minutes give no reason – they “record the new lettings without a word of explanation” – so you must put the dated facts in order.

steps.title: Find the problem
steps.text: “Six pews in the middle aisle are marked vacant that year, and four the year after.” A pew is a church bench or box seat, and to let is to rent out. So in 1848 and 1849 some pews found no one to rent them whole.

steps.title: Find the change
steps.text: “In the plan of 1851 the vacant marks are gone. Thin ruled lines now cut the boxes into single sittings, let at two shillings apiece, and names crowd where one household's name used to stand.” A sitting is a seat for one person. The empty pews disappear in the same plan in which the boxes are cut into single seats, so the single sittings are what filled them.

steps.title: See one example
steps.text: Pew 9, “an eighteen-shilling box in 1848, carries three surnames by 1856”. Where the names of one household used to stand, several households now share the box.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B fits all the facts. A brings in a shortage of seats, C says whom the sittings were meant for, which nothing in the text shows, and D gives a whole box the price of one sitting.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Single sittings were the wardens’ way of filling pews that would no longer let whole. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Names crowd” where one name used to stand, which can suggest a crowded church.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the text points to a shortage of seats. Just before the change, pews in the middle aisle stood empty: six in 1848 and four in 1849 (step 2). It is the names on the boxes that crowd, not the people in the church.

distractors.why_tempting: Two shillings is less than any whole pew cost in 1848, so the sittings sound as if they were meant for poorer families.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says whom the single sittings were meant for, or where their takers had sat before. B rests on the dated facts (steps 2 and 3), but nothing in the plans links the sittings to poorer families or shows their takers moving from the free benches.

distractors.why_tempting: Two shillings is the text’s own figure for the new lettings.
distractors.why_wrong: Two shillings bought one sitting – the sittings were “let at two shillings apiece” – not a whole box (step 3).

p5-elf-b18-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For a “concluded” question, put the dated facts in order and look for what changes together. Here the empty pews disappear in the same plan in which the single sittings appear.
p5-elf-b18-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: “Names crowd” can make you picture a full church. Read it with the vacant pews just before it: more names on a box does not mean more people than seats.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text opens with the rule that mixed-flow dryers are the ones that burn, and the count bears it out: “This is not folklore.” The rest is a quarrel about why. D names both. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the right answer must cover all its main parts, not just one paragraph.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 gives the rule – “the tall machine with the ducts inside is the one that burns” – and the count behind it: forty-four of sixty-one fires were in mixed-flow machines. Paragraphs 2 to 4 give three views of why: Calverend blames the hot shutdown at operations that dry for their neighbours as well as themselves, Grendisham questions Calverend’s timing and still finds fines in the ducts, and Steadgrove blames the end of the harvest and the contract. In paragraph 5 the writer weighs them.

steps.title: Name both halves
steps.text: The count is not in doubt, but the reason is. The right answer must name the familiar rule and the disputed account of why.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D names both. A turns one mention of a drying charge into a history of prices, B is one objection from paragraph 3, and C is an argument that the text never makes.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about a familiar rule on which dryers burn, and a disputed account of why. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does mention what drying costs, “so much per ton per point of moisture”.
distractors.why_wrong: That charge is mentioned once, to explain who buys mixed-flow machines. The text gives no prices and no change in them across the nine harvests.

distractors.why_tempting: The problem of unmanned sites is vivid, and the text ends with “no one there to watch”.
distractors.why_wrong: B is one strand of the argument: Grendisham’s objection to Calverend’s timing, which the writer takes up again at the end. The text as a whole is about why the mixed-flow machines fill the fire log (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Drying for neighbours is discussed, so a case against paying for it seems possible.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never argues that small farms should dry their own grain. Drying for others comes up only to explain who owns mixed-flow machines and works late in the harvest (step 2).

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For main-idea questions, look for the question that the whole text keeps returning to. Here every paragraph asks why one kind of dryer fills the fire log.
p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A vivid objection or a striking last sentence can look like the main point. Check whether it covers the other paragraphs too.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: Calverend’s team found that “per square foot the mixed-flow dryers carried what the cross-flow columns carried, within a few percent”. So, area for area, the two kinds were about equally dirty, which is B. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the duct swabs that Calverend’s team took, so the answer must be stated in the text. A swab is a sample wiped from a surface.

steps.title: Find the swabs
steps.text: “His team swabbed the duct faces of twenty-six machines that had never burned; per square foot the mixed-flow dryers carried what the cross-flow columns carried, within a few percent.”

steps.title: Read the result
steps.text: “Within a few percent” means almost the same. So, per square foot, the two kinds of dryer carried about the same amount of fines – “chaff, husk and broken kernel” – which is what B says.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B restates the result. A makes the mixed-flow machines far dirtier, C says that nothing had gathered, and D says that too few machines were swabbed, which nobody in the text says.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Per square foot, the two kinds of dryer came out about equally dusty. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The standard explanation says that the ducts in mixed-flow machines collect fines, so more dirt is what you would expect.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the expectation the swabs did not bear out. Per square foot, the two kinds carried the same “within a few percent” (step 2), not several times as much.

distractors.why_tempting: Grendisham mentions machines that “swabbed clean in September”, which can sound like ducts with nothing on them.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never sorts the machines by age. What Calverend’s team found was that, per square foot, the two kinds carried about the same amount (step 3), a comparison, not a finding that nothing had gathered.

distractors.why_tempting: Twenty-six machines can sound like a small sample, and cautious options often feel safe.
distractors.why_wrong: Nobody in the text says that the sample was too small. Steadgrove “accepts the swabs”, the writer calls them “hard to walk past”, and Grendisham’s doubt is about the time of year, not the number of machines.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: For “What are we told about …” questions, find the result and its exact size. Phrases such as “within a few percent” decide between options that sound alike.
p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: The familiar explanation, as in A, is what you expect to read, but the swabs went against it. Answer from the result the text reports.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: Grendisham’s point is that the time in the file is when the call came in – on an unmanned site, “when somebody looked out of a window, not when anything caught”. In Grendisham’s words: “It looks late because nobody was there to see it early.” The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what Grendisham says about the times in the fire department’s log. Find Grendisham’s objection in paragraph 3.

steps.title: Find the objection
steps.text: Grendisham says that “the clock is the weak joint in the argument”. The paragraph sets out why: “A controller log ends when the machine stops. The other time in the file is the moment the call came in. On an unmanned site at two in the morning, that is when somebody looked out of a window, not when anything caught.”

steps.title: Read Grendisham’s own words
steps.text: “Set those two numbers side by side and of course the fire looks late”, and: “It looks late because nobody was there to see it early.” So the time in the log marks when a fire was noticed, not when it began.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C restates the objection. A says that the two times agree, which is the opposite of the objection; B and D give Grendisham complaints that Grendisham never makes.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The times mark when a fire was noticed, not when it began. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A uses words from Calverend’s evidence, the burner controllers, so it sounds connected.
distractors.why_wrong: Grendisham’s point is the opposite: the two times measure different things, so “Set those two numbers side by side and of course the fire looks late” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Grendisham runs the service department of the firm that builds most of the county’s mixed-flow machines, so a limit to its own machines sounds plausible.
distractors.why_wrong: Grendisham never says this. The log is the fire department’s, and it records the sixty-one dryer fires of nine harvests; the objection is about what its times measure (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Records like a fire log are often kept for other purposes, so doubting their use as evidence sounds reasonable.
distractors.why_wrong: Grendisham never says what the log was meant for. The objection is narrower: the time in the file marks when the call came in, not when the fire began (step 2).

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question asks what a named person says, use that person’s words and the sentences that set out that person’s argument. Then match the option to the exact point being made.
p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: B and D sound like objections that someone could make, but they are not Grendisham’s. Check each option against what the person actually says.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Steadgrove argues that when the fires are sorted by date, “the machine stops mattering”: forty-nine fall in the last nine days of each harvest, when the deduction schedule “bites hardest” and the delivery window is closing. That pressure comes from the elevator’s terms, not from any machine, so growers face it then whatever they own. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that the answer is not stated outright; here you must work out what Steadgrove’s figures say about those nine days.

steps.title: Find the nine days
steps.text: Steadgrove says: “Sort the same sixty-one fires by date rather than by machine”, and “the machine stops mattering”. Then: “Forty-nine fall in a nine-day stretch at the tail of each harvest, when the deduction schedule bites hardest and the elevator’s delivery window is closing.” The elevator is the place that buys and stores the grain; its deduction schedule is its list of amounts taken off the price, and the delivery window is the time in which grain can be delivered.

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: The pressure in those days comes from the elevator’s schedule and the closing window, not from any machine. Everyone delivering grain then meets it, whatever dryer they own. That fits Steadgrove’s point that, sorted by date, “the machine stops mattering”. Custom operations simply work through that stretch, “because that is when the work is there”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A draws the one-step inference. B rounds forty-nine of sixty-one up to almost all, C gives the mutual a power that it does not have, and D turns a busy stretch into an overloaded one, which nothing in the text shows.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: In those nine days growers face the same commercial pressure, whatever machine they own. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Forty-nine of sixty-one is a large share, so it feels like nearly every fire.
distractors.why_wrong: Forty-nine of sixty-one leaves twelve fires outside the stretch, about one in five (step 2). That is too many for “Hardly a fire”.

distractors.why_tempting: The deduction schedule is the source of the pressure, and the mutual is the body that has to decide what to do.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says that Steadgrove’s remedy “is not the mutual’s to give, since the deduction schedule belongs to the elevators”. The mutual has no power to rewrite it.

distractors.why_tempting: The closing question mentions “trucks waiting”, which sounds like more grain than the dryers can handle.
distractors.why_wrong: The trucks appear only in a closing question about one imagined night, and the text does not say what they are waiting for. The tail is when “the work is there”, and the operations “run late”, but being busy is not the same as being overloaded: nothing in the text shows grain arriving faster than the dryers can take it.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “implied” questions, ask what a named cause applies to. A price schedule and a deadline set by the elevator apply to everyone delivering grain then, whatever machine they use.
p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Large shares are easy to round up. Forty-nine of sixty-one still leaves twelve fires outside the stretch, too many for “Hardly a fire”.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: In the last paragraph the writer says: “Until then Calverend’s account fits the evidence without having been tested by it.” C says the same. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s own attitude to Calverend’s explanation, not Grendisham’s or Steadgrove’s. The writer’s own voice is clearest in the last paragraph.

steps.title: Find what fits
steps.text: The writer accepts the swab result: “The swabs are hard to walk past.” The standard advice “rests on a difference in dirt that twenty-six machines failed to show”.

steps.title: Find what is missing
steps.text: “The clock is another matter. Grendisham’s objection has not been answered, and it cannot be answered from files like these; it needs a probe inside a machine that later burns, and nobody has one.” A probe is a measuring instrument. Then comes the verdict: “Until then Calverend’s account fits the evidence without having been tested by it.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches the verdict. A says that the objections have been met, B says that the writer stays out of it, and D makes the writer want a policy that the writer leaves open.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer thinks that Calverend’s explanation fits the facts but has not been tested. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer says that nobody in the argument now defends the standard advice “on the old ground”, which can make it sound as if the whole argument has gone Calverend’s way.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says plainly that one objection still stands: “Grendisham’s objection has not been answered, and it cannot be answered from files like these” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text gives three people’s views at length, which can make the writer seem neutral.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer weighs the views in the writer’s own voice: the swabs “are hard to walk past”, and Calverend’s account “fits the evidence without having been tested by it” (steps 2 and 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer calls Calverend’s remedy “nearly free”, which sounds like support for using it.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer does not go that far. Whether a run-on clause in the policies, a rule to keep the fan running after the burner stops, “would be worth anything turns on something nobody has worked out how to check”, and the text ends on a question.

p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, look for the writer’s verdict words, such as “fits the evidence” and “without having been tested”. A two-part verdict needs a two-part option.
p5-elf-b19-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Calling a remedy cheap is not recommending it. The writer notes that Calverend’s remedy is nearly free but leaves open whether writing it into next year’s policies would be worth anything.

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: To take the long view is to think about the distant future and be patient about it. The bottom of the list is “twelve years from a key”, so a new name is being asked for patience. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Whoever joins at the bottom is being asked, in the politest possible terms, to take the long ___.” The list is a waiting list for allotment plots, small pieces of land rented for growing food.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The sentences before give the numbers: fifty-eight names, four to seven plots free in an ordinary year, “which puts the bottom of the list twelve years from a key”. So whoever joins must think twelve years ahead. English says that you take the long view when you look past the present to what will happen much later.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: An outlook is a general attitude, a forecast, as in the outlook for tomorrow, or a view from a place. A gaze is a long, steady look. Sight is the ability to see, or something seen. Outlook comes closest in meaning, but the expression for patience about a distant result is take the long view, so “view” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Whoever joins at the bottom is asked “to take the long view”. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Outlook” is close in meaning to view, and people speak of a long-term outlook.
distractors.why_wrong: An outlook can be an attitude, a forecast or a view from a window, and people do speak of a long-term outlook. But the set phrase with take is to take the long view, and that fits a twelve-year wait (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A long gaze is a familiar phrase, so gaze sounds natural after long.
distractors.why_wrong: A gaze is a long, steady look. The sentence uses the set phrase for thinking far ahead, to take the long view, and a twelve-year wait asks for exactly that (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Long sight, the ability to see far-off things clearly, is a real phrase.
distractors.why_wrong: Long sight usually means seeing far-off things clearly. The frame is “take the long ___”, and the set phrase there for patience about a result twelve years away is to take the long view (step 2).

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap ends a phrase such as “to take the long ___”, think of fixed expressions with take, and check the one you find against the numbers or facts nearby.
p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: All four nouns are about seeing, so meaning alone does not decide. The expression, together with the twelve-year wait, does.

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The next sentences call the rule “the clause as written” and say that it is “simply not what the list runs on”. “Strictly” marks a statement that is true by the exact rule, even if practice differs. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, a plot cannot be inherited.” To inherit something is to receive it when its owner dies.

steps.title: Find the clue
steps.text: The sentences after the gap say: “The tenancy ends when the tenant does, and the next name on the list is written to. That is the clause as written, and nobody disputes it or finds it odd. It is simply not what the list runs on.” The rule is true on paper, but the list works in another way. Strictly, meaning by the exact rule, marks that kind of statement.

steps.title: Check the other adverbs
steps.text: “Increasingly” means more and more, but nothing in the paragraph says that the rule is changing. “Curiously” means strangely, but the text says that nobody “finds it odd”. “Privately” means in secret or personally, but the rule is the written clause. So “Strictly” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Strictly, a plot cannot be inherited.” The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The long waiting list can suggest a situation that is getting worse.
distractors.why_wrong: “Increasingly” would describe a change over time, but the paragraph presents the rule as fixed: it is “the clause as written” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A rule that the list does not run on can seem strange.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “nobody disputes it or finds it odd” (step 2). “Curiously” would call the rule strange.

distractors.why_tempting: The older hands have a private phrase, so a word about privacy seems to belong.
distractors.why_wrong: What is private is the older hands’ phrase, not the rule. The rule is “the clause as written” (step 2), and the first paragraph says: “Nothing here is hidden”.

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: For an adverb gap at the start of a sentence, read the sentences after it. Here “the clause as written” and “not what the list runs on” show that the gap marks a rule on paper.
p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: “Curiously” is tempting because the passage is wry, but the text says that nobody finds the rule odd. Check each option against what the text says.

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: To wait for dead men’s shoes is to wait for someone to die or leave so that you can take their place. That is how plots come free here: “Movement comes when somebody else stops”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “The older hands have a phrase for this among themselves, about waiting for dead men’s ___.” The older hands are the people who have held plots for a long time.

steps.title: Find the saying
steps.text: The sentence before says how plots come free: “Movement comes when somebody else stops – a knee that will not manage the walk from the gate, a move to a daughter’s town in another county, a winter that settles it.” A winter that settles it most likely hints at a death. The known English saying for this kind of wait is waiting for dead men’s shoes: waiting for someone to die or give up a place so that you can have it.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: Coats, gloves and hats are worn like shoes, and each can be handed on after a death. But the saying about waiting to take someone’s place is about shoes, and the next sentence describes it as “not affectionate”. So “shoes” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The phrase is about “waiting for dead men’s shoes”. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Coats are often handed down, and the paragraph is about inheritance.
distractors.why_wrong: The older hands use a known saying, and the saying for waiting to take someone’s place is about dead men’s shoes, not coats (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Gloves are worn like shoes and appear in other fixed phrases.
distractors.why_wrong: The saying for waiting until someone dies or leaves so that you can take their place is about shoes, not gloves (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Hats belong to the same set of worn things, and the phrase sounds just as possible with them.
distractors.why_wrong: Hats appear in other sayings, but the one for waiting to step into someone’s place is about dead men’s shoes (step 2).

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When the text says that people have “a phrase” for something, look for a known saying that matches the situation described just before.
p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: All four options are things that people wear, so any of them could follow “dead men’s”. The known saying decides, and it matches plots coming free when someone stops.

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: “Not approving, but … not ___ either” puts the gap at the other end of the scale from approving: disapproving. Censorious means strongly critical, so the line in the minutes neither approves of the change nor condemns it. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “the tone of that line is not approving, but it is not ___ either”. The line is the one line that the minutes, the written record of a meeting, give to the tenancy passing to the nephew.

steps.title: Find the scale
steps.text: A pair like “not approving, but … not ___ either” usually names the two ends of one scale and puts the thing in the middle. One end is approving, so the gap must be the other end: disapproving. Censorious means strongly critical, quick to find fault.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: Gracious means kind and polite; it is not the opposite of approving, so the sentence would have no contrast. Cautious means careful, and anxious means worried. A tone can be either, but they are about care and worry, not about approving or disapproving. So “censorious” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The tone “is not approving, but it is not censorious either”. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Gracious” is often used about tone, so it sounds natural after “not”.
distractors.why_wrong: Gracious means kind and polite. It is not the opposite of approving – if anything it leans the same way – so the “but … either” pair would set up no contrast. The gap needs the other end of the scale (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Minutes are often careful in tone, and the minutes gave the change only one line.
distractors.why_wrong: A tone can be cautious, but caution is about care, not about approval. The pair needs the opposite of approving (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A rule being stretched might worry whoever keeps the minutes, so a word for worry seems to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Anxious is about worry, not about approving or disapproving, so it does not complete the scale that the pair sets up (step 2).

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a sentence denies two things with not … but not … either, the two usually sit at opposite ends of one scale. Here one end is approving, so the gap is its opposite.
p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: “Cautious” and “anxious” can both describe a tone, which makes them feel right. Check that the word completes the scale that “approving” starts.

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The name at the top has refused three plots, and “a second refusal sends a name to the foot of the list”, yet it is still at the top. So the rule has not been used against it. To invoke a rule is to call on it and apply it. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “The rules say a second refusal sends a name to the foot of the list. The rule has not been ___.” The foot of the list is the bottom.

steps.title: Find the evidence
steps.text: “One name has stood at the top since 2019. Three plots have been offered. Three times the answer was no”. After the second refusal the rule should have sent that name to the bottom, but it is still at the top. So the rule has not been used. To invoke a rule is to call on it and apply it.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To summon is usually to order a person to come, or to gather up courage or strength. To provoke is to cause a reaction, or to make someone angry. To evoke is usually to bring a feeling, a memory or an image to mind. The sentence is about applying a rule to the name at the top, and to invoke a rule is to call on it and apply it. So “invoked” fits best.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The rule has not been invoked.” The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: To summon is also a kind of calling, and committees do summon people.
distractors.why_wrong: To summon is usually to order a person to come, or to gather courage. The sentence is about applying a rule, and to invoke a rule is to call on it and apply it (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Provoked” looks very like the key and sounds formal.
distractors.why_wrong: To provoke is to cause a reaction or to make someone angry. The sentence is not about causing a reaction; it is about a rule not being applied (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Evoked” looks and sounds very like the key, and the two words are often confused.
distractors.why_wrong: To evoke is usually to bring a feeling, a memory or an image to mind. Here the rule would be applied to a name, not brought to mind, and the facts show that it has not been applied (step 2).

p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: Use the facts around a rule to see what the sentence says about it. Three refusals and a name still at the top show that the rule has not been applied.
p5-elf-b19-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Invoke and evoke look almost the same. Invoke is used for calling on something such as a rule or a law; evoke usually means bringing a feeling or a memory to mind.
